specStatements.text: In diamond, each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms in a giant covalent structure, so diamond is very hard, has a very high melting point and does not conduct electricity.
Students should be able to explain the properties of diamond in terms of its structure and bonding.
In graphite, each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds with three other carbon atoms, forming layers of hexagonal rings which have no covalent bonds between the layers.
In graphite, one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised.
Students should be able to explain the properties of graphite in terms of its structure and bonding.
Students should know that graphite is similar to metals in that it has delocalised electrons.
Graphene is a single layer of graphite and has properties that make it useful in electronics and composites.
Students should be able to explain the properties of graphene in terms of its structure and bonding.

Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes. The structure of fullerenes is based on hexagonal rings of carbon atoms but they may also contain rings with five or seven carbon atoms. The first fullerene to be discovered was Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀ ) which has a spherical shape.
Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with very high length to diameter ratios. Their properties make them useful for nanotechnology, electronics and materials.
recognise graphene and fullerenes from diagrams and descriptions of their bonding and structure
give examples of the uses of fullerenes, including carbon nanotubes.

scopeNotes.statement: Graphene is a single layer of graphite and has properties that make it useful in electronics and composites.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Graphene is taught only as what the specification says it is - one single layer of graphite - and its properties are explained only from that structure: covalent bonds within the sheet, and one delocalised electron per carbon atom. The two application areas named by the specification, electronics and composites, are the only ones used. Nothing is taught about how graphene is manufactured, about its conductivity or strength as measured quantities, or about any electronic band theory, because the specification does not ask for any of that.

scopeNotes.statement: The first fullerene to be discovered was Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀ ) which has a spherical shape.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Buckminsterfullerene, C60, is the only fullerene named by formula anywhere in this content, and it is described exactly as the specification describes it: the first fullerene to be discovered, spherical in shape. No other individual fullerene is named or required, and carbon nanotubes are introduced only in the specification's own terms, as cylindrical fullerenes with very high length to diameter ratios. No numerical dimensions, discovery dates or people are examined.

scopeNotes.statement: so diamond is very hard, has a very high melting point and does not conduct electricity
scopeNotes.howHonoured: These three are the only properties of diamond taught, questioned or explained here, and each is traced back to the structure the specification gives: four covalent bonds from every carbon atom in a giant covalent structure. Density, refractive index, hardness scales and industrial uses of diamond are not introduced, because the specification lists these three properties and no others.

concepts.definition: A form of carbon in which each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms in a giant covalent structure. Diamond is very hard, has a very high melting point and does not conduct electricity.

A structure in which a very large number of atoms are joined to their neighbours by strong covalent bonds that run right through the substance. There are no separate small molecules, so there are no weak forces between molecules to overcome.

Every carbon atom in diamond is joined to four others by strong covalent bonds, in a rigid three-dimensional network. No atom can be pushed out of position without breaking covalent bonds, so diamond is very hard.

concepts.term: Why diamond has a very high melting point
concepts.definition: Diamond is a giant covalent structure, so melting it means breaking a very large number of strong covalent bonds. This takes a great deal of energy, so the melting point is very high.

concepts.term: Why diamond does not conduct electricity
concepts.definition: Each carbon atom in diamond uses all four of its outer electrons to form covalent bonds. There are no delocalised electrons, so there is nothing free to move through the structure and carry charge.
A form of carbon in which each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds with three other carbon atoms, forming layers of hexagonal rings.

The hexagonal rings of graphite are joined into flat layers, and there are no covalent bonds between the layers. The layers are held to one another only by weak forces of attraction, so they can slide over each other.

In graphite, one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised. Because each atom uses only three of its outer electrons in covalent bonds, the fourth is not held on one atom and is free to move through the structure, carrying charge and thermal energy.

concepts.term: Why graphite is soft and slippery
concepts.definition: There are no covalent bonds between the layers of graphite, so whole layers can slide over one another. Layers rub off easily, which is why graphite leaves a mark on paper and can act as a lubricant.

One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised, so these electrons are free to move through the structure. Moving electrons carry charge, so graphite conducts electricity, and they also carry thermal energy.

concepts.term: Why graphite has a very high melting point
concepts.definition: Within each layer the carbon atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds. A very large number of these strong bonds must be broken to melt graphite, so the melting point is very high even though graphite is soft.

concepts.term: How graphite is similar to a metal
concepts.definition: Graphite is similar to metals in that it has delocalised electrons. These delocalised electrons let graphite conduct electricity and thermal energy in the way that the delocalised electrons of a metal do, although graphite is a non-metal whose atoms are joined by covalent bonds.

A single layer of graphite: one sheet of carbon atoms, each joined to three others by covalent bonds in hexagonal rings, one atom thick. Graphene has properties that make it useful in electronics and composites.

Because graphene is a single layer of graphite, one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised, so graphene conducts electricity, which makes it useful in electronics. Every atom in the sheet is held by strong covalent bonds, so graphene is very strong for its mass, which makes it useful in composites.
A molecule of carbon atoms with a hollow shape. The structure of fullerenes is based on hexagonal rings of carbon atoms, but they may also contain rings with five or seven carbon atoms.
The first fullerene to be discovered, C60, which has a spherical shape.

A cylindrical fullerene with a very high length to diameter ratio, which means the tube is extremely long compared with how wide it is. Their properties make carbon nanotubes useful for nanotechnology, electronics and materials.

Fullerenes are hollow, so other molecules can be held inside the cage, which is used to deliver drugs into the body. They have a large surface area, so they can be used as catalysts, and they are also used as lubricants. Carbon nanotubes are used in nanotechnology and electronics, and are added to materials to reinforce them, for example in tennis racket frames.

Graphene is drawn or described as a single flat sheet of hexagonal rings, one atom thick, with no layers above or below it. Fullerenes are drawn or described as closed hollow shapes, a ball or a tube, built mainly from hexagonal rings and sometimes containing rings of five or seven carbon atoms. Graphite is drawn as several such sheets stacked in layers.

misconceptions.question: Why is graphite soft enough to write with?
misconceptions.correct: There are no covalent bonds between the layers of graphite, so whole layers slide over one another. The covalent bonds inside each layer are strong and are not broken.
misconceptions.misconception: Graphite is soft because the covalent bonds in graphite are weak.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students link soft to weak. Because graphite rubs off onto paper they assume whatever holds it together must be feeble, and they never separate the bonding inside a layer from the forces between layers.
misconceptions.correction: Ask where the sliding happens. Graphite gives way between the layers, where there are no covalent bonds at all. Inside each layer the covalent bonds are strong, which is why graphite still has a very high melting point.

misconceptions.question: What has to be broken to melt diamond?
misconceptions.correct: A very large number of strong covalent bonds. Diamond is a giant covalent structure, not a substance made of separate molecules, so there are no weak forces between molecules to overcome.
misconceptions.misconception: Diamond is covalent, so it is made of molecules held together by weak forces, and those weak forces are what you overcome when it melts.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Simple molecular substances are taught alongside diamond and both are covalent. Students carry across the rule that covalent substances melt easily because the forces between the molecules are weak.
misconceptions.correction: Check first whether the substance is made of separate molecules. Diamond has none; the covalent bonds run through the whole crystal, so they are the bonds that must be broken, and that is why the melting point is very high.

misconceptions.question: Why can diamond not conduct electricity?
misconceptions.correct: All four outer electrons of every carbon atom are used in covalent bonds, so there are no delocalised electrons free to move and carry charge.
misconceptions.misconception: Diamond does not conduct because there are no electrons in diamond.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students shorten 'no free electrons' to 'no electrons' when they revise, and they are rarely asked to say what the electrons in diamond are doing instead.
misconceptions.correction: Always say what the electrons are doing. In diamond all four outer electrons are held in bonds; in graphite one per atom is delocalised, and that single difference is why graphite conducts and diamond does not.

misconceptions.question: What carries the current when graphite conducts electricity?
misconceptions.correct: Delocalised electrons carry the charge. One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised and free to move through the structure.
misconceptions.misconception: Graphite conducts because its layers slide over each other and carry the current along.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both softness and conduction are explained from the layer structure, so students fuse the two explanations and use the movement of layers to account for the movement of charge.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the two properties apart. Softness comes from there being no covalent bonds between the layers; conduction comes from the one delocalised electron contributed by each carbon atom.

misconceptions.question: Does graphite have a high or a low melting point?
misconceptions.correct: Very high. The carbon atoms within each layer are joined by strong covalent bonds and a very large number of them must be broken for graphite to melt.
misconceptions.misconception: Graphite is soft, so it must melt at a low temperature.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Hardness and melting point are both treated as 'how tough is it', so a soft solid is assumed to be easy to melt as well.
misconceptions.correction: Hardness and melting point measure different things. Graphite gives way between its layers, which makes it soft, but melting it means breaking the strong covalent bonds inside the layers.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the fourth outer electron of each carbon atom in graphite?
misconceptions.correct: It is delocalised. One electron from each carbon atom is free to move through the whole structure instead of staying on one atom.
misconceptions.misconception: Each carbon atom in graphite has a spare fourth electron, and it stays put in the outer shell of its own atom.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Bonding is first taught with electrons drawn in fixed shells, so a spare electron is pictured sitting where it started, and delocalised is read as merely meaning 'not used in a bond'.
misconceptions.correction: Delocalised means the electron is no longer attached to any one atom. That is precisely why graphite conducts electricity and why graphite is described as being similar to a metal.

misconceptions.question: Is graphite a metal?
misconceptions.correct: No. Graphite is a form of carbon, a non-metal, whose atoms are joined by covalent bonds. It is similar to metals only in that it has delocalised electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Graphite conducts electricity and has delocalised electrons, so graphite must be a metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conducting electricity is the test students use to identify a metal, and delocalised electrons are first met in metallic bonding, so both clues point them the wrong way.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states a similarity, not an identity: graphite is similar to metals in that it has delocalised electrons. Its atoms are still held by covalent bonds, and carbon is a non-metal.

misconceptions.question: Is graphene a fullerene?
misconceptions.correct: No. Graphene is a single layer of graphite, a flat sheet of hexagonal rings one atom thick. Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes.
misconceptions.misconception: Graphene, fullerenes and nanotubes are all the same sort of thing, so graphene is a hollow cage of carbon too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: All three are met in the same lesson as new forms of carbon built from hexagonal rings, so students file them under a single heading and stop distinguishing them.
misconceptions.correction: Sort them by shape. Graphene is a flat sheet one atom thick with nothing above or below it. A fullerene is a closed hollow shape, which is why a nanotube counts as a fullerene but a graphene sheet does not.

misconceptions.question: Is graphene strong?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Every carbon atom in the sheet is joined to three others by strong covalent bonds, so graphene is very strong for its mass, which is why it is useful in composites.
misconceptions.misconception: Graphene is only one atom thick, so it must be weak and tear easily.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Thin things in everyday life tear, and students judge the sheet by how thick it is rather than by the bonds holding its atoms together.
misconceptions.correction: Judge strength from the bonding. The sheet is thin, but every bond in it is a strong covalent bond, so adding graphene to a composite strengthens it without adding much mass.

misconceptions.question: Do all fullerenes have the same shape and size as C60?
misconceptions.correct: No. Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes of many kinds. Buckminsterfullerene, C60, was simply the first one to be discovered and it is the one with a spherical shape.
misconceptions.misconception: Every fullerene is a sphere made of exactly 60 carbon atoms.
misconceptions.whyItArises: C60 is usually the only fullerene students see drawn, and the football picture is so memorable that it becomes their definition of the whole family.
misconceptions.correction: What defines a fullerene is a hollow shape built mainly from hexagonal rings, not a particular number of atoms. Carbon nanotubes are fullerenes too, and they are cylinders.

misconceptions.question: Which ring sizes can a fullerene contain?
misconceptions.correct: The structure of fullerenes is based on hexagonal rings of carbon atoms, but they may also contain rings with five or seven carbon atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: Fullerenes are built from hexagonal rings only, exactly like graphite and graphene.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Hexagonal rings dominate every diagram of graphite and graphene, so students carry the rule over and do not notice the other ring sizes in a fullerene.
misconceptions.correction: Look for the odd rings in a fullerene diagram. Rings of five or seven carbon atoms sit among the hexagons, and they are what let a flat arrangement of rings close up into a hollow shape.

misconceptions.question: Are carbon nanotubes fullerenes?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with very high length to diameter ratios.
misconceptions.misconception: Fullerenes are the ball-shaped ones, so a nanotube must belong to some other family of carbon structures.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word fullerene is introduced with a picture of a sphere, so students treat the round shape rather than the hollow carbon cage as the defining feature, and then need a separate box for tubes.
misconceptions.correction: Fullerene covers any molecule of carbon atoms with a hollow shape. A nanotube is a fullerene that has been drawn out into a cylinder rather than closed into a ball.

misconceptions.question: What does a very high length to diameter ratio tell you about a carbon nanotube?
misconceptions.correct: That the tube is very long compared with how wide it is. The diameter is on the nanometre scale, so a nanotube is extremely thin, not large.
misconceptions.misconception: A high length to diameter ratio means the tube is enormous, so nanotubes are long thick fibres you could see and handle.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read the word length and think about absolute size, forgetting that a ratio compares two measurements of the same object against each other.
misconceptions.correction: A ratio compares. Length divided by diameter is very large because the diameter is tiny, and it is that extreme thinness that makes nanotubes useful in nanotechnology.

misconceptions.question: What are diamond and graphite made from?
misconceptions.correct: Both are made from carbon atoms and nothing else. They differ in how those atoms are bonded: four covalent bonds from each carbon atom in diamond, three in graphite.
misconceptions.misconception: Diamond and graphite behave so differently that they must contain different elements, or graphite must have something extra mixed into it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two substances look and behave nothing alike, so students assume the difference must come from different ingredients rather than from a different arrangement of the same atoms.
misconceptions.correction: Compare the bonding, not the ingredients. Each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds in diamond and three in graphite, and that difference alone accounts for every property in the specification.

misconceptions.question: What is between the layers of graphite?
misconceptions.correct: No covalent bonds at all. The layers of hexagonal rings are held to each other only by weak forces of attraction, which is why they slide.
misconceptions.misconception: The layers of graphite must be joined by covalent bonds too, just weaker ones than the bonds inside a layer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students expect anything that holds a solid together to be bonds of some kind, and a 'weak covalent bond' feels like a sensible compromise between the layers being joined and the layers sliding.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is precise: layers of hexagonal rings which have no covalent bonds between the layers. Every covalent bond in graphite lies inside a layer.

mcqs.stem: In diamond, how many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form, and with what?

options.text: Four covalent bonds, within a small carbon molecule
options.rationale: Students who treat every covalent substance as molecular get the number of bonds right but picture diamond as separate molecules.

options.text: Four covalent bonds, with four other carbon atoms
options.rationale: The specification states that in diamond each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms.

options.text: Four covalent bonds, with atoms of other elements
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume something other than carbon must be present to explain diamond's properties.

options.text: Three covalent bonds, with three other carbons
options.rationale: This is graphite's figure, recalled for the wrong form of carbon because the two are learned together.

mcqs.stem: Why does diamond not conduct electricity?

options.text: The carbon atoms in diamond do not contain any electrons
options.rationale: The revision shorthand 'no electrons' is taken literally, when what is missing is delocalised electrons.

options.text: Its molecules are packed too tightly for electrons to move
options.rationale: Picked by students who picture diamond as molecules and explain conduction by how closely they sit.

options.text: All four outer electrons of each carbon atom are held in bonds
options.rationale: With every outer electron used in a covalent bond there are no delocalised electrons free to move and carry charge.

options.text: The covalent bonds in diamond are far too strong to break
options.rationale: A true fact about the bonds, offered as an explanation of conduction, which depends on free electrons rather than bond strength.

mcqs.stem: Diamond has a very high melting point. What is the reason?

options.text: The weak forces between the diamond molecules must be overcome
options.rationale: The simple molecular rule is applied to a giant structure that contains no molecules at all.

options.text: A very large number of strong covalent bonds must be broken
options.rationale: Diamond is a giant covalent structure, so melting it means breaking huge numbers of strong covalent bonds.

options.text: Diamond has no free electrons to carry energy through it
options.rationale: The explanation for non-conduction is reached for and used to answer a question about melting.

options.text: The carbon atoms in diamond are unusually heavy atoms
options.rationale: Melting point is confused with atomic mass; carbon atoms are in fact light.

mcqs.stem: Which feature of diamond's structure explains why it is very hard?

options.text: The layers of carbon atoms are unable to slide past each other
options.rationale: The layer explanation belongs to graphite; diamond has no layers, so this reasoning is imported wholesale.

options.text: There are no delocalised electrons anywhere in the structure
options.rationale: True of diamond, but it explains why diamond does not conduct, not why it is hard.

options.text: The carbon atoms are much smaller than the atoms of a metal
options.rationale: Atom size is offered instead of bonding; small atoms do not by themselves make a substance hard.

options.text: Every atom is held in place by four strong covalent bonds
options.rationale: The rigid three-dimensional network means no atom can move without covalent bonds being broken.

mcqs.stem: In graphite, each carbon atom forms:

options.text: three covalent bonds, plus weak covalent bonds between layers
options.rationale: Students want something bonding the layers together and invent a weaker covalent bond to do it.

options.text: four covalent bonds, as in every other form of carbon
options.rationale: Diamond's figure is generalised to all carbon, which would leave no delocalised electron.

options.text: three covalent bonds, forming layers of hexagonal rings
options.rationale: This is the specification's description of graphite: three covalent bonds with three other carbon atoms, forming layers of hexagonal rings.

options.text: two covalent bonds, forming long chains of carbon atoms
options.rationale: Chosen by students who remember that graphite is not four-bonded and guess downwards to a chain structure.

mcqs.stem: What lies between the layers of hexagonal rings in graphite?

options.text: No covalent bonds at all, only weak forces of attraction
options.rationale: The specification states that the layers have no covalent bonds between them, which is why they slide.

options.text: Weak covalent bonds, which are broken easily by rubbing
options.rationale: The layers clearly hold together somehow, so a weakened covalent bond feels like the obvious answer.

options.text: The fourth outer electron of each atom, fixed in position
options.rationale: The spare electron is placed between the layers and pictured as staying still rather than being delocalised.

options.text: Covalent bonds that are weaker than the ones in diamond
options.rationale: Softness is explained by comparing bond strengths with diamond instead of by the absence of bonds.

mcqs.stem: In graphite, one electron from each carbon atom is:

options.text: delocalised, and free to move through the structure
options.rationale: The specification states that in graphite one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised.

options.text: left on its own atom, in the outer shell where it began
options.rationale: The fixed-shell picture from earlier bonding work survives, so the electron is imagined staying put.

options.text: used to bond weakly to the layer above and below
options.rationale: The spare electron is given the job of holding the layers together, which is not what the specification says.

options.text: lost completely, leaving the carbon atom positively charged
options.rationale: The metallic bonding picture of positive ions in a sea of electrons is transferred to graphite.

mcqs.stem: Graphite is soft enough to leave a mark on paper. Why?

options.text: The covalent bonds within graphite are weak and break easily
options.rationale: Soft is equated with weakly bonded, ignoring the strong bonds within each layer.

options.text: Its delocalised electrons let the atoms slip past each other
options.rationale: The delocalised electrons are used to explain every property of graphite, including this one.

options.text: Its layers can slide because no covalent bonds join them
options.rationale: With no covalent bonds between the layers, whole layers slide over one another and rub off.

options.text: It melts at a low temperature, so it wears away very easily
options.rationale: Softness and a low melting point are treated as the same property.

options.text: One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised and moves
options.rationale: Delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure, and moving electrons carry charge.

options.text: Its layers slide over each other and carry the charge
options.rationale: The sliding-layer explanation is reused for conduction because both come from the layer structure.

options.text: Each carbon atom holds a spare electron in its outer shell
options.rationale: The spare electron is recognised but is imagined as staying on its own atom, which would not carry charge.

options.text: It is a metal, and every metal conducts electricity well
options.rationale: Conduction is taken as proof that graphite is a metal, which reverses the reasoning.

mcqs.stem: Graphite is soft, yet its melting point is very high. Why?

options.text: Its melting point is in fact low, which is why it is soft
options.rationale: The premise of the question is rejected because soft and easily melted are held to be the same.

options.text: The covalent bonds within each layer are strong and numerous
options.rationale: Melting graphite means breaking a very large number of the strong covalent bonds inside the layers.

options.text: The weak forces between layers must be broken to melt it
options.rationale: The forces that make graphite soft are wrongly identified as the ones broken on melting.

options.text: Its delocalised electrons carry heat out of the solid
options.rationale: Delocalised electrons are invoked again, this time to explain a melting point.

mcqs.stem: In what way is graphite similar to a metal?

options.text: Graphite is a metal, so it behaves in the same way
options.rationale: A similarity is upgraded into an identity; carbon is a non-metal.

options.text: Graphite is held together by metallic bonds as well
options.rationale: Delocalised electrons are assumed to mean metallic bonding, but graphite's atoms are joined covalently.

options.text: Graphite contains a small amount of metal in its layers
options.rationale: An extra ingredient is invented to account for graphite behaving unlike a typical non-metal.

options.text: Graphite has delocalised electrons, as metals do
options.rationale: The specification states that graphite is similar to metals in that it has delocalised electrons.

options.text: a hollow ball of carbon atoms, like a fullerene
options.rationale: Graphene and fullerenes are met together and merged into one idea.

options.text: a single layer of graphite, one atom thick
options.rationale: The specification defines graphene as a single layer of graphite.

options.text: a stack of graphite layers, very thinly sliced
options.rationale: Chosen by students who remember graphene is thin but not that it is a single layer.

options.text: a compound of carbon with another element
options.rationale: The name sounds like a compound, so an extra element is assumed to be present.

mcqs.stem: Why is graphene useful in electronics and in composites?

options.text: It is one atom thick, so it bends and stretches very easily
options.rationale: Thinness is read as weakness, so graphene is credited with the wrong property.

options.text: It is hollow, so other substances can be held inside it
options.rationale: A property of fullerenes is transferred to graphene, which is a flat sheet, not a cage.

options.text: It is a metal, and metals conduct well and are very strong
options.rationale: Conduction is again taken as evidence of metallic character rather than of delocalised electrons.

options.text: It has delocalised electrons and strong covalent bonds
options.rationale: One delocalised electron per carbon atom lets it conduct, and the strong covalent bonds make it strong for its mass.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about fullerenes is correct?

options.text: They are built from hexagonal rings of carbon and nothing else
options.rationale: The hexagon rule learned for graphite and graphene is carried over without exception.

options.text: They are all spheres containing exactly 60 carbon atoms
options.rationale: C60 is the only fullerene most students picture, so it becomes the definition of the family.

options.text: They are hollow molecules based on hexagonal rings of carbon
options.rationale: The specification describes fullerenes as molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes, based on hexagonal rings.

options.text: They are giant covalent structures like diamond and graphite
options.rationale: Fullerenes are grouped with the other carbon structures, but they are molecules, not giant structures.

options.text: A cylinder with a very high length to diameter ratio
options.rationale: The named fullerene is confused with the other fullerene the specification describes, the nanotube.

options.text: A sphere of 60 atoms, and the only shape a fullerene takes
options.rationale: The correct description of C60 is spoiled by the claim that no other fullerene shape exists.

options.text: A flat sheet of hexagonal rings, sixty carbon atoms across
options.rationale: The hexagon-sheet image of graphene is applied, missing the hollow shape entirely.

options.text: The first fullerene discovered, C60, with a spherical shape
options.rationale: This is exactly what the specification states about Buckminsterfullerene.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about carbon nanotubes is correct?

options.text: They are not fullerenes, because fullerenes are spherical
options.rationale: The sphere is treated as the defining feature of a fullerene, so tubes are excluded.

options.text: Their high length to diameter ratio makes them wide tubes
options.rationale: The ratio is read as a statement about size rather than about shape.

options.text: They are cylindrical fullerenes, very long and very thin
options.rationale: The specification describes carbon nanotubes as cylindrical fullerenes with very high length to diameter ratios.

options.text: They are one atom thick, so they are weak and bend easily
options.rationale: Thinness at the nanoscale is again taken to mean the structure must be flimsy.

mcqs.stem: A diagram shows a flat sheet of hexagonal carbon rings, one atom thick, with no layers above or below it. What does the diagram show?

options.text: A fullerene, because fullerenes are sheets of hexagons
options.rationale: Fullerenes and graphene are not separated, so any hexagonal sheet is called a fullerene.

options.text: Graphene, a single layer of graphite one atom thick
options.rationale: A single layer of hexagonal rings with nothing above or below it is exactly graphene.

options.text: Graphite, because graphite is made of hexagonal rings
options.rationale: The hexagonal rings are recognised but the single layer, rather than a stack, is overlooked.

options.text: A nanotube, viewed from the side as a flattened sheet
options.rationale: A cylinder is imagined drawn flat, so the tube is read into a sheet diagram.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is an example of a use of fullerenes?

options.text: Making thick cables that can be seen with the naked eye
options.rationale: The length to diameter ratio is read as meaning nanotubes are large objects.

options.text: Acting as a single flat sheet inside touchscreen glass
options.rationale: A graphene application is offered because graphene and fullerenes are not distinguished.

options.text: Burning in oxygen to release energy as a cheap fuel
options.rationale: Fullerenes are carbon, so combustion feels plausible, but it is not a use given for them.

options.text: Delivering drugs into the body inside their hollow cages
options.rationale: Fullerenes are hollow, so molecules can be held inside the cage and carried into the body.

mcqs.stem: Carbon nanotubes are added to the frame of a tennis racket. Why?

options.text: They are very strong, so they reinforce the material used
options.rationale: Their strength is why nanotubes are added to materials, one of the uses the specification names.

options.text: They are thin, so they let the frame bend much more easily
options.rationale: Nanoscale thinness is taken to mean the tubes must weaken or soften the material.

options.text: They are wide tubes, so they fill the space inside the frame
options.rationale: The high length to diameter ratio is misread as the tubes being broad.

options.text: They are soft and slippery, so they reduce friction in it
options.rationale: The sliding-layer property of graphite is transferred to nanotubes.
